lore_summary.en: Thirty years. Sixty thousand verses. A tomb in Tus. The Shahnameh outlives every king it describes.
lore_summary.fa: فردوسی سی سال بدون سفارش رسمی شاهنامه را نوشت. سلطان محمود به جای طلا، نقره فرستاد — توهینی دقیق که فردوسی را به تبعید راند. گفته می‌شود طلا روزی رسید که تشییع جنازه‌اش از در دیگر شهر بیرون می‌رفت. در باغ خودش دفن شد. شعرش هنوز در هر عروسی و عزا خوانده می‌شود.

scenes.body_en: Ferdowsi was from Tus, in Khorasan — a landowner by birth, a poet by vocation, and a man who spent thirty years writing a poem no one had asked him to write. He began it while the Samanid dynasty still gave Persian culture institutional support. He finished it under Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni, a Turkic ruler whose court spoke Arabic and who had little feel for what he had been given.

The famous story is this: Mahmud had promised gold for each verse of the Shahnameh. When Ferdowsi presented the completed poem — sixty thousand couplets, thirty years of work — Mahmud sent silver instead. The insult was precise, the same kind of precise insult the Shahnameh itself knew how to recognize: the distaff sent to Bahram Chubin, the disrespect calibrated to wound exactly. Ferdowsi wrote a bitter satire against the sultan, was warned his life was in danger, and fled. He spent years in exile. By some accounts, Mahmud eventually sent the gold — a camel train of it — and it arrived at Tus the same day Ferdowsi's funeral procession was leaving through one gate of the city.

Whether that story is precisely true matters less than what it preserves: the image of a man who gave everything to a work that his own age could not fully receive. The Shahnameh was too large, too honest, too rooted in a world the Ghaznavid court was not interested in. It found its audience later — in the Seljuk courts, in the Persian diaspora, in the illustrated manuscripts of the Timurid and Safavid eras, in the living rooms of Iranian families across fifteen centuries.

Ferdowsi died around 1020 CE, probably in his eighties, having written the longest poem ever composed by a single poet. He asked to be buried outside the main cemetery because the Shahnameh contained material a strict religious authority might have found objectionable. He was buried in his own garden. The poem he left behind is still read, still memorized, still recited at weddings and funerals and at the moment when an Iranian wants to reach for the deepest thing in the language.

battle.intro_en: Thirty years. Sixty thousand verses. A patron who paid in silver when he owed gold. Ferdowsi's legacy was built despite the court, not because of it. To face this gate you must understand how the Shahnameh survived its own creation.
